# 1.1 Population and Demography

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Demography** is the study of the size, structure, growth, distribution, and movement of a population.

## World population clusters

| Cluster | Region |
|---|---|
| **Major** | **East Asia** — China, Japan (the Tokaido corridor), Korea |
| **Major** | **South Asia** — India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka |
| **Major** | **Europe** — the UK through western Russia |
| **Secondary** | Southeast Asia, northeastern USA |

Nearly all of these are **temperate, low-lying, well-watered, and coastal or riverine** — the conditions for intensive agriculture, and now for trade.

## The demographic measures

| Measure | Definition | Calculation |
|---|---|---|
| **CBR** — Crude Birth Rate | Live births per 1,000 population per year | (births ÷ population) × 1,000 |
| **CDR** — Crude Death Rate | Deaths per 1,000 population per year | (deaths ÷ population) × 1,000 |
| **TFR** — Total Fertility Rate | Average children a woman has in her lifetime | — |
| **ASFR** — Age-Specific Fertility Rate | Live births per 1,000 women in a specific age group per year | — |
| **IMR** — Infant Mortality Rate | Infant (under 1 year) deaths per 1,000 live births | (infant deaths ÷ live births) × 1,000 |
| **NIR** — Natural Increase Rate | Population growth **excluding migration** | (CBR − CDR) ÷ 10, as an annual % |
| **MMR** — Maternal Mortality Ratio | Maternal deaths per 100,000 live births | — |

**What raises and lowers each:**

- **TFR falls** with **female empowerment**, contraception, economic pressure, and changing norms
- **Birth rates fall** with **economic development, female education, contraception access, urbanisation**, and the **high cost of raising children**
- **Death rates fall** with **medical advances, public health, nutrition**, and living standards
- **IMR falls** with **prenatal and postnatal care, immunisation, nutrition, hygiene**, and education

The single most consistent predictor of falling fertility is **female education**. It operates through several channels at once — later marriage, better access to contraception, higher opportunity cost of childbearing — which is why it appears in almost every list above.

**Which measure shows the greatest health disparity between LDCs and MDCs — CBR, CDR, or TFR?**

**None of them: the maternal mortality ratio.** The gap in maternal deaths between rich and poor countries is far larger, proportionally, than the gap in any other common measure — because maternal death is almost entirely preventable with basic obstetric care, so its rate reflects health-system quality more directly than any other statistic.

## Dependency ratios

The **dependency ratio** measures the proportion of **non-working-age people** (children and elderly) to **working-age** people, highlighting the potential economic pressure on those who work.

**High dependency ratio:** a larger proportion of dependents, meaning more economic pressure on the working-age population through taxes and family support.

**Youth dependency ratio** — people aged 0–14 relative to those aged 15–64. It indicates the burden of supporting children through **education, healthcare, and family services**.

**Elderly (old-age) dependency ratio** — people aged 65 and over relative to those aged 15–64. It indicates the burden of **pensions, healthcare**, and other needs of a retired population.

Splitting the ratio matters because the two halves have opposite time signatures. A high **youth** ratio is temporary and becomes an economic advantage when that cohort reaches working age; a high **elderly** ratio is permanent and grows.

## The Demographic Transition Model

| Stage | Name | Birth rate | Death rate | Growth | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | High Stationary | High | High | Stable or slow | Pre-industrial societies, e.g. 18th-century Europe |
| **2** | Early Expanding | High (25+/1,000) | **Falling** (~15/1,000) | **Rapid** | Britain 1750s–late 19th c.; Bangladesh, Nigeria today |
| **3** | Late Expanding | **Falling** | Low | Slowing | Industrialising economies |
| **4** | Low Stationary | Low | Low | Stable | Developed economies |

**Stage 2 is where the population explosion happens**, and the cause is asymmetric timing: **death rates fall first** — through improved sanitation, food production and storage, medical advances, and lower infant mortality — while birth rates take a generation or more to adjust. The gap between the two curves is the growth.

### Key assumptions of the DTM

1. **Linear progression** — all countries follow the same path from Stage 1 to Stage 4 as they develop economically
2. **Industrialisation-driven** — declining death and birth rates are tied to technological and social advancement
3. **No migration impact** — the model ignores migration's role entirely

All three are questionable, and the exam will reward saying so. The model was built from European experience and assumes every country repeats it.

### Stage 5?

Some scholars propose a **Stage 5 (post-industrial decline)**, in which **birth rates fall below death rates**, causing a natural **decrease** in population. Examples include **Japan, Germany, and Italy**, where deaths exceed births but total population is often maintained by **immigration**.

**Criticism:** because the DTM does not account for migration, Stage 5 remains debated — the countries in question are shrinking naturally but not actually shrinking.

### Relating the DTM to population pyramids

Each stage has a characteristic pyramid shape: a **wide-based triangle** in Stages 1–2 (many children, few elderly), a **narrowing base** in Stage 3, and a **column or inverted shape** in Stage 4–5 as the elderly cohort grows and the base contracts.

## Demographic momentum

A **large young population** produces **high demographic momentum**: even after fertility falls to replacement level, the population **continues growing for decades**, because a large cohort of young people is still entering childbearing age.

This is why fertility policy takes so long to show results, and why a country can have below-replacement fertility and a growing population at the same time.

## Malthus

Malthus argued that **population grows geometrically** (2, 4, 8, 16…) while **food supply grows arithmetically** (2, 4, 6, 8…). The imbalance would lead to:

- **Positive checks** — famine and disease
- **Preventative checks** — late marriage

**Criticism:**

- **Technological advances**, notably the **Green Revolution**, disproved his food-scarcity predictions
- He **ignored global trade** and the role of **family planning** in population control

Malthus's arithmetic was not wrong; his assumption that agricultural output could not grow faster than linearly was. That is the standard shape of failed predictions in this field — the logic holds and the premise about technology does not.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Demography** | The study of the size, structure, growth, distribution, and movement of a population |
| **CBR (Crude Birth Rate)** | Live births per 1,000 population per year |
| **CDR (Crude Death Rate)** | Deaths per 1,000 population per year |
| **TFR (Total Fertility Rate)** | Average children a woman has in her lifetime |
| **ASFR (Age-Specific Fertility Rate)** | Live births per 1,000 women in a specific age group per year |
| **IMR (Infant Mortality Rate)** | Infant (under 1 year) deaths per 1,000 live births |
| **NIR (Natural Increase Rate)** | Population growth excluding migration, calculated as (CBR − CDR) ÷ 10 and given as an annual percentage |
| **MMR (Maternal Mortality Ratio)** | Maternal deaths per 100,000 live births |
| **Dependency ratio** | The proportion of non-working-age people (children and elderly) to working-age people, highlighting the potential economic pressure on those who work |
| **High dependency ratio** | A larger proportion of dependents, meaning more economic pressure on the working-age population through taxes and family support |
| **Youth dependency ratio** | People aged 0–14 relative to those aged 15–64; it indicates the burden of supporting children through education, healthcare, and family services |
| **Elderly (old-age) dependency ratio** | People aged 65 and over relative to those aged 15–64; it indicates the burden of pensions, healthcare, and other needs of a retired population |
| **Stage 1: High Stationary** | High birth rate, high death rate, stable or slow growth — pre-industrial societies |
| **Stage 2: Early Expanding** | High birth rate (25+/1,000) with a falling death rate (~15/1,000), giving rapid growth |
| **Stage 3: Late Expanding** | Falling birth rate, low death rate, slowing growth |
| **Stage 4: Low Stationary** | Low birth rate, low death rate, stable population — developed economies |
| **Stage 5 (post-industrial decline)** | A proposed stage in which birth rates fall below death rates, causing a natural decrease in population |
| **Demographic momentum** | The effect by which a large young population keeps a population growing for decades even after fertility falls to replacement level, because a large cohort is still entering childbearing age |
| **Positive checks** | Famine and disease |
| **Preventative checks** | Late marriage |

# 2.1 Migration

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Ravenstein's Laws

Ravenstein derived a set of empirical regularities about migration that still hold reasonably well:

1. **Most migration is over a short distance.** Migrants tend to move short distances, often within the same region or country.
2. Migration proceeds **step by step**, in stages, rather than in one long move.
3. **Long-distance migrants** head for the **great centres of commerce and industry**.
4. Each migration flow produces a **counter-flow** in the opposite direction.
5. **Rural** inhabitants are more migratory than **urban** ones.
6. Within a country, **females** migrate more than males; **internationally**, males predominate.
7. **Most migrants are adults**, not families with children.
8. Large towns grow **more by migration than by natural increase**.
9. Migration **increases with economic development** and improved transport.
10. Migration is **mostly economic** in motive.

Because migrants tend to move short distances and along established routes, **communities of people from the same origin form in the new location** — chain migration, which then makes subsequent migration from that origin easier still.

## Push and pull factors

Migration is analysed as a balance between **push factors** (reasons to leave) and **pull factors** (reasons to come), usually grouped by category:

| Category | Push (reasons to leave) | Pull (reasons to come) |
|---|---|---|
| **Economic** | High unemployment, poverty, low wages | Money, jobs, financial opportunity, higher standard of living |
| **Political** | Persecution, war, oppression | Stability, freedom, safety |
| **Social** | Discrimination, lack of services | Family and community, education, healthcare |
| **Environmental** | Drought, flood, natural disaster, degradation | Favourable climate, fertile land |

Push and pull factors rarely operate alone. The people who leave a country in economic crisis are typically not the poorest — migration costs money — which is one of the reasons development can **increase** emigration in the short term before reducing it.

## The three intervening concepts

Three ideas explain why a push and a pull do not automatically produce a migration:

**Intervening obstacle.** A barrier that makes the journey harder or impossible — a border, a mountain range, a visa requirement, the cost of travel. It considers the **costs and effort involved in making the move**.

**Intervening opportunity.** An attractive place **along a migrant's intended route** that causes them to **stop there instead of reaching the original destination**. This is a large part of why Ravenstein's step migration occurs: migrants aim far and stop when something good enough appears.

**Complementarity.** One place has something another place needs. For migration this usually means one area has a **surplus of people or skills** while another has a **demand for them**. Without complementarity there is no reason for a flow at all, however strong the push.

The three work in sequence: complementarity creates the potential for migration, intervening opportunities redirect it, and intervening obstacles reduce it.

## Brain drain

The migration of skilled professionals from poorer to richer countries **depletes the healthcare workforce in the origin countries**, weakening their health systems and worsening health outcomes.

The dynamic is self-reinforcing and difficult to address: a country that invests in training doctors loses that investment to countries that did not make it, which reduces its capacity to train more. It is one of the clearest cases where an individually rational decision produces a collectively damaging outcome.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Step migration** | Migration that proceeds step by step, in stages, rather than in one long move |
| **Chain migration** | Communities of people from the same origin forming in the new location, which then makes subsequent migration from that origin easier still |
| **Push factors** | Reasons to leave — unemployment, poverty and low wages; persecution, war and oppression; discrimination and lack of services; drought, flood, disaster and degradation |
| **Pull factors** | Reasons to come — money, jobs and a higher standard of living; stability, freedom and safety; family, education and healthcare; favourable climate and fertile land |
| **Intervening obstacle** | A barrier that makes the journey harder or impossible — a border, a mountain range, a visa requirement, the cost of travel; it considers the costs and effort involved in making the move |
| **Intervening opportunity** | An attractive place along a migrant's intended route that causes them to stop there instead of reaching the original destination |
| **Complementarity** | One place has something another place needs — usually one area has a surplus of people or skills while another has a demand for them |
| **Brain drain** | The migration of skilled professionals from poorer to richer countries, which depletes the healthcare workforce in the origin countries, weakening their health systems and worsening health outcomes |
